newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Jobless claims shine alone.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Jobless claims shine alone.

text.p: U.S. credit markets will likely remain rangebound Thursday as Wall Street, still loaded with recently acquired fresh Treasury supply, grapples with yet another day of scarce economic data.

"Tomorrow is really pretty light. It's just jobless claims," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc, referring to the release at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT of initial jobless claims data for the week ended October 19.
In a Reuters survey, economists expect claims to drop to 336,000 from 340,000 in the prior seven-day period.
Analysts said, however, players are not expected to rely much on this week's claims since the data might have been affected by some special factors.

They said the numbers might be distorted by a 20-day-long strike of General Motors auto workers in Canada, which shut some GM plants in the U.S. GM and the Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) agreed to settle the strike on Tuesday with a new three-year contract.
"We've got the affects of the Canadian auto strike ... So I think no one is going to be changing any views based on tomorrow's information," Glassman said.

Analysts said the market weathered the flood of fresh supply early in the week, which ended with the sale of $12.5 billion of five-year T-notes on Wednesday. The Treasury placed the securities at 6.325 percent. Bid-to-cover ratio was 2.33.

The market, which had spent most of the morning and midday trade in negative territory, rallied mildly after the auction results were announced. The buying bout was welcome, but some analysts dropped a word of caution.
"The money which entered the market after the auction was mostly foreign central bank buying," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
"So if the buying dries up tomorrow, we might see prices lagging again. The Street is still fairly loaded with fresh paper," the trader added.
Market watchers also said players are gearing up for the release of new, more substantial data on Friday, including the durable goods and the existing home sales reports for September.

"We're now in the middle of a trading range and I don't think the market will be inclined to move strongly one way or the other at least until Friday morning," said Jerry Zukowski, money market economist at PaineWebber Inc.
The U.S. Treasury market has been trading in a fairly broad range for more than two weeks now as players await fresh key numbers to crunch.
Analysts see the yield on the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond is seen staying between 6.70 percent and 6.85 percent.
"The odds are that we're going to stay where we are. But if we move, I don't think we'll break any technical patterns here," said another trader at a primary dealership.
In late Wednesday trade, the bellwether bond was quoted up 10/32 at 98-31/32 to yield 6.83 percent.

The Federal Reserve added reserves to the money market on Wednesday via overnight system repurchase agreements when the federal funds rate was at 5-1/2 percent, well above the central bank's 5-1/4 percent target.
Federal funds are expected to open at 5.25 percent on Thursday, analysts said.
